questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Statistical Thermodynamics & Electrochemistry (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: In the high-temperature classical rotational partition function $q_{\text{rot}}$, the rotational symmetry numbers ($\sigma$) of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, $\text{NH}_3$, and $\text{CH}_4$ are, respectively:
questions.explanationEn: The rotational symmetry number $\sigma$ equals the order of the pure rotational subgroup (number of proper rotations, including $E$) of the molecule's point group. For $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ($C_{2v}$), proper rotations are $E, C_2 \implies \sigma = 2$. For $\text{NH}_3$ ($C_{3v}$), $E, 2C_3 \implies \sigma = 3$. For $\text{CH}_4$ ($T_d$), $E, 8C_3, 3C_2 \implies \sigma = 12$.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Statistical Thermodynamics & Electrochemistry (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: Which one of the following particles obeys Bose-Einstein statistics?
questions.explanationEn: Particles with integer total spin ($0, 1, 2, \dots$) are bosons and obey Bose-Einstein statistics, whereas particles with half-integer spin ($1/2, 3/2, \dots$) are fermions obeying Fermi-Dirac statistics. A $^4\text{He}$ atom consists of $2$ protons, $2$ neutrons, and $2$ electrons (even number of fermions, total spin $0$), making it a boson.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Statistical Thermodynamics & Electrochemistry (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: The abnormally high limiting ionic molar conductivity of $\text{H}^+$ ($349.8\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}$) in water at $298\text{ K}$ compared to $\text{Na}^+$ ($50.1\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}$) is primarily due to:
optionsEn: The very small hydrated radius of $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ moving via classical Stokesian drift
Complete absence of hydration around the bare proton
Proton hopping along hydrogen-bonded water chains (Grotthuss mechanism)
questions.explanationEn: Rather than migrating solely as a bulky hydrated $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ ion by hydrodynamic drift, a proton transfers rapidly from one water molecule to an adjacent hydrogen-bonded water molecule via bond cleavage and formation (the Grotthuss proton-hopping mechanism), resulting in an exceptionally large effective mobility.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Statistical Thermodynamics & Electrochemistry (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: When a weak acid ($\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$) is titrated conductometrically with a weak base ($\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$), the conductance after the equivalence point:
optionsEn: Remains almost constant because excess $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ is weakly ionized
Decreases sharply due to common-ion suppression
Increases sharply due to excess $\text{OH}^-$ ions
questions.explanationEn: Up to the equivalence point, weakly dissociated $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ is converted into the strong electrolyte salt $\text{CH}_3\text{COONH}_4$, so conductance rises. Beyond the equivalence point, excess $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ is a weak base whose ionization is further suppressed by the $\text{NH}_4^+$ already present, so conductance remains nearly flat.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Statistical Thermodynamics & Electrochemistry (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: In a potentiometric titration where cell potential $E$ is plotted against volume $V$ of titrant added, the equivalence point is most accurately identified as the volume where:
optionsEn: The second derivative $\frac{d^2 E}{dV^2}$ reaches a maximum
The first derivative $\frac{dE}{dV}$ reaches a sharp extremum (maximum or minimum) and $\frac{d^2 E}{dV^2} = 0$
questions.explanationEn: In a potentiometric titration, the potential $E$ undergoes a steep sigmoidal jump across the equivalence point. This inflection point corresponds to a sharp peak (extremum) in the first-derivative plot $dE/dV$ vs $V$, and a zero-crossing ($d^2E/dV^2 = 0$) in the second-derivative plot.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Statistical Thermodynamics & Electrochemistry (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following statements comparing the Einstein and Debye models for the heat capacity of monoatomic crystalline solids is/are CORRECT?
optionsEn: Both models recover the classical Dulong-Petit limit $C_{V,m} \to 3R$ at high temperatures ($T \gg \Theta$).
The Einstein model assumes all $3N$ oscillators vibrate with a single frequency $\nu_E$, whereas the Debye model assumes a continuous spectrum of frequencies up to a cutoff $\nu_D$.
The Einstein model accurately reproduces the experimental $T^3$ dependence of $C_{V,m}$ at very low temperatures.
questions.explanationEn: Both models converge to $3R$ at high $T$ (A) and vanish as $T \to 0$ (B). Einstein used a single frequency $\nu_E$, whereas Debye used a continuous acoustic spectrum up to $\nu_D$ (C). At very low $T$, the Einstein model decays too rapidly (exponentially, $e^{-\Theta_E/T}$), whereas only the Debye model reproduces the experimental $T^3$ law (D is false).

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Statistical Thermodynamics & Electrochemistry (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following statements regarding concentration cells at constant temperature is/are CORRECT?
optionsEn: For any concentration cell, the standard cell EMF $E_{\text{cell}}^\circ$ is identically zero.
In an electrode (amalgam or gas) concentration cell, the driving force is the difference in activity of the electrode material at the two electrodes.
In an electrolyte concentration cell with transference, the EMF depends on the transport number of the ion that does NOT participate in the electrode reaction.
An electrolyte concentration cell without transference has a non-zero liquid junction potential.
questions.explanationEn: Because both half-cells use the same electrode couple, $E_{\text{cell}}^\circ = E^\circ - E^\circ = 0$ (A). Electrode concentration cells are driven by activity differences in amalgam/gas electrodes (B). For electrolyte concentration cells with transference (e.g., $\text{H}_2|\text{HCl}(a_1)|\text{HCl}(a_2)|\text{H}_2$, electrodes reversible to $\text{H}^+$), $E = 2t_-\frac{RT}{F}\ln(a_{\pm,2}/a_{\pm,1})$, depending on $t_-$ of the non-electrode ion $\text{Cl}^-$ (C). Cells without transference have no liquid-liquid junction ($E_j = 0$, D is false).

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Statistical Thermodynamics & Electrochemistry (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: At $298\text{ K}$, the limiting ionic molar conductivities of $\text{K}^+$ and $\text{Br}^-$ in water are $73.5$ and $78.1\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}$, respectively. The transport number of $\text{K}^+$ in an infinitely dilute aqueous $\text{KBr}$ solution (rounded off to three decimal places) is _______.
questions.explanationEn: The transport number of the cation $\text{K}^+$ at infinite dilution is $t_+^\circ = \frac{\lambda_+^\circ}{\lambda_+^\circ + \lambda_-^\circ} = \frac{73.5}{73.5 + 78.1} = \frac{73.5}{151.6} = 0.485$.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Statistical Thermodynamics & Electrochemistry (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: A heteronuclear diatomic gas has a characteristic rotational temperature $\Theta_{\text{rot}} = 2.0\text{ K}$. Using the high-temperature approximation, its rotational partition function $q_{\text{rot}}$ at $300\text{ K}$ (in integer) is _______.
questions.explanationEn: For a heteronuclear diatomic molecule, the symmetry number is $\sigma = 1$. In the high-temperature limit ($T \gg \Theta_{\text{rot}}$), $q_{\text{rot}} = \frac{T}{\sigma \Theta_{\text{rot}}} = \frac{300}{1 \times 2.0} = 150$.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Statistical Thermodynamics & Electrochemistry (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: The standard reduction potential for $\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}$ at $298\text{ K}$ is $E^\circ = 0.340\text{ V}$. Assuming activity equals molar concentration and $\frac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.059\text{ V}$, the reduction potential of a $\text{Cu}$ electrode immersed in $0.010\text{ M Cu}^{2+}$ solution (in $\text{V}$, rounded off to three decimal places) is _______.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Statistical Thermodynamics & Electrochemistry (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: For an ideal gas-phase isomerization equilibrium $\text{A}(\text{g}) \rightleftharpoons \text{B}(\text{g})$, where $\Delta \varepsilon_0 = \varepsilon_{0,B} - \varepsilon_{0,A}$ is the difference in ground-state (zero-point) energies between $\text{B}$ and $\text{A}$, the equilibrium constant $K$ is given by:
questions.explanationEn: At equilibrium, $\mu_A = \mu_B$. Using $\mu_i = \varepsilon_{0,i} - k_B T \ln(q_i / N_i)$ (where $q_i$ is evaluated relative to each molecule's own ground state), equating $\mu_A = \mu_B$ yields $k_B T \ln\left(\frac{N_B}{N_A}\right) = k_B T \ln\left(\frac{q_B}{q_A}\right) - (\varepsilon_{0,B} - \varepsilon_{0,A})$, hence $K = \frac{N_B}{N_A} = \frac{q_B}{q_A} e^{-\Delta \varepsilon_0 / (k_B T)}$.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Statistical Thermodynamics & Electrochemistry (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: A mobile ideal gas molecule of mass $m$ adsorbed on a flat solid surface of area $\mathcal{A}$ translates freely in two dimensions. Its 2D translational partition function $q_{\text{trans, 2D}}$ is:
questions.explanationEn: For each translational degree of freedom of length $L$, the 1D partition function is $q_{1\text{D}} = \left(\frac{2\pi m k_B T}{h^2}\right)^{1/2} L$. For 2D translation over area $\mathcal{A} = L_x L_y$, $q_{\text{trans, 2D}} = q_x q_y = \left(\frac{2\pi m k_B T}{h^2}\right) \mathcal{A}$.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Statistical Thermodynamics & Electrochemistry (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: Given the standard reduction potentials $E^\circ(\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}^+) = +0.15\text{ V}$ and $E^\circ(\text{Cu}^+/\text{Cu}) = +0.52\text{ V}$ in aqueous solution at $298\text{ K}$, the standard reduction potential $E^\circ(\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu})$ and stability of $\text{Cu}^+(\text{aq})$ are:
questions.explanationEn: Using additivity of $\Delta G^\circ$: $2 E^\circ(\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}) = 1(0.15) + 1(0.52) = 0.67\text{ V} \implies E^\circ(\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}) = +0.335\text{ V}$. For disproportionation $2\text{Cu}^+ \to \text{Cu}^{2+} + \text{Cu}$, $E_{\text{disp}}^\circ = E^\circ(\text{Cu}^+/\text{Cu}) - E^\circ(\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}^+) = 0.52 - 0.15 = +0.37\text{ V} > 0$, so $\text{Cu}^+(\text{aq})$ spontaneously disproportionates.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Statistical Thermodynamics & Electrochemistry (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: Consider two $\text{HCl}$ concentration cells between the same activities $a_1$ and $a_2$ using $\text{H}_2(\text{g})|\text{Pt}$ electrodes: Cell I has transference ($E_t$), and Cell II has no transference using $\text{Ag}|\text{AgCl}$ intermediate electrodes ($E_{wt}$). The ratio $E_t / E_{wt}$ is equal to:
questions.explanationEn: For Cell I (with transference, electrodes reversible to $\text{H}^+$), $E_t = 2t_- \frac{RT}{F}\ln\left(\frac{a_{\pm,2}}{a_{\pm,1}}\right)$. For Cell II (without transference), $E_{wt} = 2\frac{RT}{F}\ln\left(\frac{a_{\pm,2}}{a_{\pm,1}}\right)$. Taking their ratio directly gives $\frac{E_t}{E_{wt}} = t_-$, which is a standard potentiometric method to measure transport numbers.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Statistical Thermodynamics & Electrochemistry (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: When a strong electrolyte solution is subjected to a very high electric field ($\sim 10^5\text{ V cm}^{-1}$), its molar conductivity increases toward $\Lambda_m^\circ$ because ions move faster than the ionic atmosphere can reform. This phenomenon is called the:
questions.explanationEn: Under an extremely high electric field, ions travel so rapidly that they escape their ionic atmosphere, eliminating both the relaxation and electrophoretic drag and raising $\Lambda_m$ toward $\Lambda_m^\circ$; this is the **Wien effect**. By contrast, the increase in conductivity under very high-frequency alternating fields is the **Debye-Falkenhagen effect**.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Statistical Thermodynamics & Electrochemistry (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: For an ideal gas of $N$ indistinguishable non-interacting molecules with $Q(N, V, T) = \frac{q^N}{N!}$ and $q = q_{\text{trans}}(V,T)\,q_{\text{int}}(T)$, which of the following statements is/are CORRECT?
optionsEn: The pressure $P = k_B T \left(\frac{\partial \ln Q}{\partial V}\right)_{N,T} = \frac{N k_B T}{V}$ depends only on $q_{\text{trans}}$ and is independent of $q_{\text{int}}$.
The internal energy $U$ is the sum of translational and internal contributions: $U = U_{\text{trans}} + U_{\text{int}}$.
The entropy $S$ is the sum of translational and internal contributions: $S = S_{\text{trans}} + S_{\text{int}}$.
The factor $1/N!$ enters the internal entropy $S_{\text{int}}$ rather than the translational entropy $S_{\text{trans}}$.
questions.explanationEn: Because only $q_{\text{trans}} \propto V$ depends on volume, $P = k_B T (\partial \ln Q / \partial V)_{N,T} = N k_B T / V$ (A). Since $\ln Q = (N\ln q_{\text{trans}} - \ln N!) + N\ln q_{\text{int}}$, both $U$ (B) and $S$ (C) separate additively into translational and internal parts, with the indistinguishability factor $1/N!$ conventionally grouped with $q_{\text{trans}}$ (D is false).

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Statistical Thermodynamics & Electrochemistry (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: For a liquid junction between two concentrations $a_1$ and $a_2$ of the same $1:1$ electrolyte $\text{MX}$ (written as $\text{MX}(a_1) \mid \text{MX}(a_2)$), which of the following statements about the liquid junction potential $E_j = \phi_2 - \phi_1$ is/are CORRECT?
optionsEn: If $t_+ = t_- = 0.5$, the liquid junction potential vanishes ($E_j = 0$).

For $\text{HCl}(0.1\text{ M}) \mid \text{HCl}(0.01\text{ M})$, since $t_{\text{H}^+} > t_{\text{Cl}^-}$, the dilute side ($0.01\text{ M}$) becomes positively charged relative to the concentrated side.
The liquid junction potential is independent of temperature $T$.
questions.explanationEn: For a $1:1$ electrolyte junction $\text{MX}(a_1) \mid \text{MX}(a_2)$, $E_j = \phi_2 - \phi_1 = (t_+ - t_-)\frac{RT}{F}\ln\left(\frac{a_{\pm,1}}{a_{\pm,2}}\right)$ (A). Thus $E_j = 0$ when $t_+ = t_-$ (B), and $E_j$ is directly proportional to $T$ (D is false). When $a_1 > a_2$ for $\text{HCl}$, faster $\text{H}^+$ ions outpace $\text{Cl}^-$ diffusing into the dilute side, making the dilute side positive ($\phi_2 > \phi_1$, C).

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Statistical Thermodynamics & Electrochemistry (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: A diatomic molecule has a characteristic vibrational temperature $\Theta_v = 600\text{ K}$. Taking the $v = 0$ level as the zero of energy, the vibrational partition function $q_v$ at $T = 600\text{ K}$ (rounded off to three decimal places) is _______.
questions.explanationEn: With the energy zero at $v = 0$, $q_v = \frac{1}{1 - e^{-\Theta_v/T}}$. At $T = \Theta_v = 600\text{ K}$, $\Theta_v/T = 1$, so $q_v = \frac{1}{1 - e^{-1}} = \frac{1}{1 - 0.36788} = \frac{1}{0.63212} = 1.582$.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Statistical Thermodynamics & Electrochemistry (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: At $298\text{ K}$, the standard reduction potentials are $E^\circ(\text{Ag}^+/\text{Ag}) = +0.800\text{ V}$ and $E^\circ(\text{AgBr}/\text{Ag},\text{Br}^-) = +0.071\text{ V}$. Taking $\frac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.0591\text{ V}$, the value of $\text{p}K_{sp} = -\log_{10} K_{sp}$ for $\text{AgBr}$ at $298\text{ K}$ (rounded off to two decimal places) is _______.
questions.explanationEn: For the dissolution $\text{AgBr}(\text{s}) \rightleftharpoons \text{Ag}^+(\text{aq}) + \text{Br}^-(\text{aq})$ ($n = 1$), $E_{\text{cell}}^\circ = E^\circ(\text{AgBr}/\text{Ag},\text{Br}^-) - E^\circ(\text{Ag}^+/\text{Ag}) = 0.071 - 0.800 = -0.729\text{ V}$. Using $E_{\text{cell}}^\circ = \frac{0.0591}{n}\log_{10} K_{sp}$, we obtain $\text{p}K_{sp} = -\log_{10} K_{sp} = -\frac{E_{\text{cell}}^\circ}{0.0591} = \frac{0.729}{0.0591} = 12.34$.

questions.pyqTag: GATE CY Topic • Statistical Thermodynamics & Electrochemistry (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: For a single-step, one-electron electrode reaction at $298\text{ K}$ with exchange current density $j_0 = 1.00\text{ mA cm}^{-2}$ and symmetry factor $\alpha = 0.50$, an anodic overpotential of $\eta = +0.1182\text{ V}$ is applied. Using the Butler-Volmer equation with $\frac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.0591\text{ V}$, the net anodic current density $j$ (in $\text{mA cm}^{-2}$, rounded off to two decimal places) is _______.
questions.explanationEn: Writing the Butler-Volmer equation in base-$10$ form: $j = j_0\left[10^{(1-\alpha)\eta / 0.0591} - 10^{-\alpha\eta / 0.0591}\right]$. With $\alpha = 0.50$ and $\frac{\eta}{0.0591} = \frac{0.1182}{0.0591} = 2.00$, the exponents are $+1.00$ and $-1.00$. Thus $j = 1.00\,(10^1 - 10^{-1}) = 1.00\,(10 - 0.1) = 9.90\text{ mA cm}^{-2}$.
